title: WHY DO WE CALL JESUS “LORD” WHILE NEGOTIATING WHICH OF HIS COMMANDS WE WILL FOLLOW?
paragraphs: WHY DO WE CALL JESUS “LORD” WHILE NEGOTIATING WHICH OF HIS COMMANDS WE WILL FOLLOW?
The Most Dangerous Kind of Disobedience May Be the One We Have Learned to Justify — And the Most Terrifying Words We Could Ever Hear May Come from the Savior We Claimed to Know.

You can sing about Jesus with tears in your eyes, defend His name in public, post Bible verses every morning, attend church faithfully, and still spend much of your life resisting the very One you call Lord.
Not because you openly hate Him.
Not because you have abandoned Christianity.
But because somewhere along the way, you began treating His commandments like suggestions that needed your approval.
You obey when His Word comforts you.
You agree when His teaching supports your decisions.
You celebrate His promises when you need a miracle.
But when His Word confronts your pride, your secret relationships, your bitterness, your dishonesty, your appetite for revenge, your love of money, or the sin you have quietly decided to keep...
Suddenly, you need more time to pray about it.
Suddenly, you want another interpretation.
Suddenly, obedience becomes complicated.
And the question we desperately need to face is not whether we know how to call Jesus Lord.
It is whether we have surrendered the right to tell Him no.
Because one day, every excuse we have carefully rehearsed will stand before the One who sees straight through it.
And there is something Jesus said that should disturb anyone who has learned to sound surrendered while remaining secretly in control.
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” — Luke 6:46, ESV
Read that again.
Jesus was not speaking to people who had never heard His name.
He was confronting the contradiction between what people confessed with their mouths and what they practiced with their lives.
They knew what to call Him.
But their obedience told another story.
And perhaps that is why this verse feels so uncomfortable.
Because some of us have become remarkably skilled at giving Jesus the title while withholding the throne.
We want a Savior who forgives us.
But we hesitate before a Lord who commands us.
We want His peace without surrendering our grudges.
His blessing without surrendering our idols.
His presence without surrendering our private compromises.
His forgiveness without forgiving the people who wounded us.
His kingdom without allowing His kingship to rearrange our lives.
And the tragedy is not that Jesus has failed to make His will known.
The tragedy is that we sometimes understand exactly what He is asking...
And start negotiating anyway.
In the Greek text of Luke 6:46, Jesus asks:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
A close translation is:
“But why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do the things I say?”

The word Κύριε (Kyrie) is the form of Kyrios used when addressing someone. Depending on context, kyrios can mean master, sir, or lord. Here, Jesus is confronting people who address Him as their authority while refusing to act upon His words.
And ποιεῖτε (poieite) comes from poieō, meaning to do, make, or carry out.
Notice what Jesus does not ask.
He does not ask, “Why do you call Me Lord when you are still struggling?”
He does not ask, “Why do you call Me Lord when you have not achieved perfection?”
He asks why they call Him Lord while failing to do what He says.
The issue is not whether a genuine disciple ever falls.
The issue is whether we have made peace with refusing the One we claim to follow.
There is a difference between a believer who stumbles and cries out for mercy and a person who deliberately protects disobedience while demanding that God approve it.
One is fighting sin.
The other is negotiating its continued residence.
And if that distinction makes you uncomfortable, do not rush past it.
Sometimes the mercy of God begins by disturbing the peace we have made with what is destroying us.
Think about the last time Scripture confronted something you did not want to surrender.
Maybe it was a relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it was the way you spoke to your spouse when nobody else was listening.
Maybe it was the resentment you kept feeding because forgiving someone felt like allowing them to escape accountability.
Maybe it was a dishonest business practice that had become so normal you no longer called it dishonesty.
Maybe it was the sexual temptation you kept returning to, promising yourself that the next time would be the last.
Or maybe it was something much quieter.
The hunger to be admired.
The refusal to apologize.
The secret satisfaction when someone who hurt you finally suffered.
The pride that made correction feel like persecution.
The habit of being spiritually impressive in public while emotionally cruel at home.
You knew what Scripture said.
You felt the conviction.
And instead of asking, “Lord, how do I obey You?” you began asking, “How far can I go without technically disobeying?”
That is a dangerous question.
Because it reveals that our hearts may be searching for the boundary of rebellion rather than the beauty of holiness.
And before anyone misunderstands, this is not a message declaring that every Christian who struggles with sin is a hypocrite.
If that were true, none of us could stand.
The apostle John wrote to believers:
“If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, ESV
But he immediately pointed us toward hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, ESV
The Gospel does not teach that Christians never sin.
It teaches that sin is no longer something we can comfortably enthrone.
Grace does not mean we stop needing repentance.
Grace brings us back to the Savior who forgives, cleanses, and transforms.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because there was a man who called Jesus Lord, promised extraordinary loyalty, and then failed when it mattered most.
His name was Peter.
Peter was not a stranger to Jesus.
He had walked with Him.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard teachings that generations would treasure.
He had seen the sick healed and the impossible become possible.
When Jesus warned His disciples that they would fall away, Peter was certain he would remain faithful.
Even if everyone else failed, Peter believed he would stand.
Yet before the night was over, the man who had promised to remain loyal denied knowing Jesus three times.
Not once.
Three times.
And when the rooster crowed, Luke records a detail that still breaks the heart:
“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” — Luke 22:61, ESV
Imagine that moment.
The face of the One who had loved him.
The eyes of the One who had warned him.
The Lord he had promised never to abandon.
Peter remembered.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come because we have been caught.
And there are tears that come because we finally see what our sin has done to a relationship we treasure.
Peter's tears were not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter's love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The disciple who had publicly denied Jesus was not beyond restoration.
But notice something beautiful.
Jesus did not restore Peter by declaring that denial was harmless.
He restored him through a love that confronted his failure and called him forward into faithful service.
This is the Gospel.
Not pretending that our rebellion was never rebellion.
Not minimizing the commands of Christ.
Not teaching wounded people that they must become flawless before approaching God.
But announcing that the crucified and risen Savior receives repentant sinners and makes new beginnings possible.
Peter's failure was real.
Christ's mercy was greater.
And someone reading this needs to hear that.
You may have denied Jesus through your choices even while professing Him with your words.
You may have compromised in ways that nobody knows.
You may have returned to a sin you promised to abandon.
You may have damaged relationships, wasted opportunities, or carried a secret that makes you feel unworthy even to pray.
But your failure does not have to become your final identity.
The same Jesus who confronted Peter also restored him.
And He has not lost His power to restore those who turn back to Him.
Still, restoration is not permission to continue living as though His words do not matter.
Because Jesus never separated love from obedience.
In John 14:15, He said:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.” — ESV
The Greek reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) comes from agapaō, meaning to love.
The word τηρήσετε (tērēsete) comes from tēreō, meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
The form translated “you will keep” expresses what follows from love. The surrounding passage also connects loving Jesus with keeping His word.
Jesus was not selling salvation in exchange for perfect performance.
He was describing the relationship between genuine love and a life that takes His words seriously.
Obedience is not the price by which we purchase God's love.
It is a fitting response to the love we have received.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works.
But the very next verse says that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for them to walk in.
Grace saves us apart from our merit.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us unchanged.
This matters because two terrible misunderstandings have wounded countless souls.
One says, “If you fail, Jesus no longer wants you.”
The other says, “Because Jesus forgives, it does not matter how you live.”
Both distort the Gospel.
The first forgets His mercy.
The second forgets His lordship.
The truth is far more beautiful and far more demanding.
Jesus receives sinners who cannot save themselves.
And He calls those He receives to follow Him.
Not to earn the cross.
But because of the cross.
Not to manufacture righteousness through human effort.
But because the Holy Spirit is at work transforming those who belong to Christ.
Paul addressed this very issue in Romans 6:1–2:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” — ESV
Grace is not heaven's approval of the sin that enslaves us.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, bringing forgiveness and new life.
And sometimes that new life begins with the most difficult word a human heart can speak.
Yes.
Yes, Lord, even when obedience costs me.
Yes, Lord, even when I have to admit I was wrong.
Yes, Lord, even when I have to end what I have been secretly defending.
Yes, Lord, even when forgiveness feels impossible without Your help.
Yes, Lord, even when following You means disappointing people whose approval I desperately wanted.
Yes, Lord, even when nobody applauds.
Because calling Jesus Lord is not merely giving Him an honored place in our religious vocabulary.
It is acknowledging that His authority reaches into the places we would rather keep locked.
And here is something that should make us examine our hearts even more carefully.
We can sometimes obey the commands that cost us little while resisting the commands that threaten what we love most.
We can give generously while refusing to reconcile.
We can defend biblical morality while speaking with contempt toward people made in God's image.
We can quote Scripture accurately while using it to crush others instead of speaking truth in love.
We can preach repentance to strangers while refusing to confess our own sin to the people we have hurt.
We can condemn the sins we do not struggle with while carefully excusing the sins we do.
And because our visible obedience looks impressive, we begin believing that the hidden areas no longer matter.
But God sees the whole person.
Jesus rebuked religious leaders who were careful about certain outward duties while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23).
He did not teach that outward obedience was meaningless.
He taught that religious precision cannot excuse a heart that neglects what matters deeply to God.
That should humble all of us.
Because it is possible to be correct about a biblical doctrine and still be disobedient in the way we treat the person sitting across from us.
It is possible to know the language of holiness while refusing the humility holiness requires.
It is possible to win an argument about Christ and fail to reflect His character during the argument.
And perhaps one of the most revealing tests of our discipleship is not how passionately we defend Jesus before people who agree with us.
It is how willingly we obey Him when His words correct us.
Especially when nobody is watching.
Especially when obedience is inconvenient.
Especially when our pride has something to lose.
This is why the warning in Matthew 7:21–23 is so sobering.
Jesus said that not everyone who addresses Him as Lord will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of His Father.
He described people appealing to remarkable religious works done in His name, only to hear Him declare that He never knew them.
This is not a passage inviting anxious believers to despair every time they stumble.
It is a warning against confusing religious activity with a genuine relationship of faith and obedience.
Spiritual accomplishments cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Public ministry cannot purchase salvation.
Even extraordinary works cannot make a life of lawlessness acceptable to God.
And there is a question worth asking before we ever speak about the sins of the world.
What if the most dangerous deception is not believing that Jesus is unimportant...
But believing that calling Him Lord is the same as following Him?
James gives us another unsettling image.
He compares someone who hears God's Word without acting upon it to a person who looks in a mirror and then walks away, forgetting what he looks like (James 1:22–24).
Think about that.
Scripture exposes what needs attention.
We see it.
We recognize it.
We feel the discomfort.
Then we close the Bible, return to our routines, and behave as though nothing was revealed.
We become collectors of sermons rather than doers of the Word.
We save Christian videos but ignore the truth they contain.
We repost warnings about sin while hiding the habits that are slowly hardening our hearts.
And eventually, even conviction can become familiar.
We feel it, admire the message, perhaps even cry over it...
Then refuse to change.
Tears can be sincere.
But tears alone are not repentance.
Biblical repentance involves turning toward God, a changed mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
The New Testament often uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, a word associated with a change of mind and turning from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling terrible about what we have done.
It is responding to God's truth by turning from sin and trusting Him.
That does not mean transformation is always instant.
Some battles involve years of learning, accountability, confession, and dependence on the Holy Spirit.
Some wounds require time and wise support to heal.
Some patterns must be confronted repeatedly as believers learn to walk in freedom.
But there is a difference between struggling toward obedience and planning to remain disobedient.
A struggling believer says, “Lord, help me surrender what I cannot seem to release.”
A negotiating heart says, “Lord, I will surrender everything except this.”
And Jesus loves us too much to pretend that the difference is unimportant.
Consider the rich young ruler in Mark 10.
He approached Jesus with a serious question about eternal life.
He had an outward record of commandment-keeping.
But Jesus exposed the attachment that held his heart.
Mark 10:21 says something astonishing before describing Jesus' challenge.
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Then He told the man to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him.
This was a particular command addressed to a particular man, revealing his attachment to wealth. It does not mean every Christian is commanded to sell every possession.
But it reveals a principle none of us can safely ignore.
The thing we refuse to surrender may expose what we are trusting more than Christ.
And the young man went away sorrowful because he had great possessions.
He was close enough to hear the invitation.
But he walked away.
Not because Jesus hated him.
Jesus loved him.
And that love did not prevent Jesus from telling him the truth.
We often want love to mean that God will never confront what we treasure.
But sometimes His love confronts the very thing that threatens to master us.
For one person, it may be money.
For another, reputation.
For another, sexual sin.
For another, bitterness.
For another, control.
For another, the desperate need to be right.
The question is not whether everyone must surrender the same particular possession or circumstance.
The question is whether there is anything we insist must remain beyond the authority of Christ.
Because the moment we declare, “Jesus, You may have everything except this,” we have identified a place where our hearts still need to yield.
And that is not a reason to run away from Him.
It is a reason to come closer.
Look at the cross.
Really look.
The Son of God did not enter our broken world to offer a convenient religious lifestyle.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died and rose again.
He did what no sinner could do to reconcile us to God.
And when we consider the price of our redemption, how can we treat His words as though they were optional advice from someone who has no claim upon our lives?
We are not saved because our obedience is impressive.
We are saved because Christ is sufficient.
But the One who saves us is also the One who calls us to follow.
The cross is not a bargain in which Jesus gives us forgiveness while we reserve the right to remain our own masters.
It is the place where mercy meets our deepest need and where the old claim of sin upon our lives is decisively challenged.
Paul wrote:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV
Those words are not meant to erase our human dignity.
They remind believers that redemption changes our belonging.
Our bodies, our choices, our relationships, and our daily lives matter to the Lord who redeemed us.
And if you are feeling convicted right now, please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to perform enough religious activities to make Jesus accept you.
The answer is to come to Jesus.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Stop defending what His Word calls sin.
Ask Him for the grace to obey.
Seek help from mature believers when you need accountability.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Apologize where you have wronged someone.
Forgive as Christ commands, without confusing forgiveness with permission for further abuse or the abandonment of wise boundaries.
And when you stumble, do not turn your failure into an excuse to abandon Him.
Return to the Savior.
Again.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His mercy is real.
And His transforming grace is stronger than the lie that you can never change.
There is a beautiful promise in Ezekiel 36:26–27.
God promises His people a new heart and a new spirit, and speaks of putting His Spirit within them, causing them to walk in His statutes.
In the Hebrew text, the expression לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash) means “a new heart.”
And רוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה (ruach chadashah) means “a new spirit.”

These words appear in a promise originally addressed to Israel concerning God's cleansing and restoration. Christians understand the promised work of the Spirit in light of the new covenant accomplished through Jesus Christ.
The hope is not simply that people will become better at pretending to be holy.
It is that God Himself changes hearts.
He does not merely demand outward conformity while leaving His people helpless.
He gives His Spirit to those who belong to Christ.
This is why true Christian obedience is not merely willpower wearing religious clothing.
It is the fruit of faith, love, and the Holy Spirit's transforming work.
And that is wonderful news for the person who has tried to change and failed a hundred times.
You do not need another mask.
You need the mercy and power of the living Christ.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony.
You need to tell the truth before God.
You do not need to convince everyone that you are already healed.
You need to keep walking with the One who heals.
And perhaps tonight, that begins with a prayer you have been avoiding.

“Jesus, I have called You Lord while resisting Your Word. I have defended what You have been calling me to surrender. I have wanted Your comfort without always welcoming Your correction. Forgive me. Give me a heart that loves You more than my excuses. Teach me to obey, not to earn Your love, but because You first loved me. By Your Spirit, change what I cannot change on my own. Amen.”
No dramatic music.
No public performance.
Just a heart finally telling the truth.
And maybe that is where the greatest turning point happens.
Not when everybody sees you becoming religious.
But when nobody sees you choosing obedience.
When you delete the message you know you should not send.
When you admit the truth instead of protecting your image.
When you walk away from temptation before it becomes another regret.
When you refuse to feed the bitterness that has been poisoning your soul.
When you choose faithfulness over applause.
When you open Scripture not to find a loophole, but to hear your Lord.
When you whisper, “Jesus, I do not fully understand why this is so hard, but I want to follow You.”
Those moments may never become viral testimonies.
But they matter.
Because discipleship is lived in the ordinary decisions where love becomes action.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to turn your confession into a public spectacle.
But perhaps you can take one honest step.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to pretend you have mastered every struggle.
But as a simple confession that you want Jesus to rule the places you have been reluctant to surrender.
And if you have experienced the restoring mercy of Jesus after a season of compromise, consider sharing a testimony of what His grace has done.
Someone reading the comments may believe they are too far gone.
Your testimony may remind them that repentance is still possible and that Christ has not stopped receiving those who come to Him.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to produce words that stir emotions for a moment.
Not simply to collect reactions, views, or applause.
But to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, the necessity of repentance, the wonder of grace, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
We live in a world where distraction is endless and biblical truth can easily become another piece of content that disappears beneath tomorrow's entertainment.
Yet people are still searching.
A father wondering how to rebuild his family after years of spiritual neglect.
A mother praying over a child who has walked away from faith.
A young believer struggling with temptation and afraid to admit it.
A husband and wife trying to learn forgiveness.
A person who has never opened a Bible but secretly wonders whether God could love someone with their past.
And sometimes a single Scripture-centered message, encountered at the right moment, becomes the beginning of a conversation that changes a life.
That is why sharing this article matters.
Not because you owe anyone a performance of faith.
But because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the very question you have just faced.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to explore Gospel Warrior for daily Scripture, biblical truth, encouragement, conviction, and discipleship.
Not as another religious post to collect.
Return to Luke 6:46.
Return to John 14:15.
Return to the cross.
Remember that the Savior who commands you is the Savior who gave Himself for you.
These resources and gifts can also become opportunities to encourage meaningful conversations about faith in everyday life.
But the deepest value of joining is not the discount.
It is the opportunity to help make more Christ-centered encouragement and biblical discipleship available to others.
Our prayer is that these resources will encourage you to study Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen your faith, and become more firmly rooted in Christ.
You can still participate in this mission.
Read Scripture.
Pray for this ministry.
Use the free resources.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Love your neighbor.
Remain faithful to your local church.
The Gospel is not for sale, and the grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
It is to help point a community toward the Lord Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Why do we call Jesus Lord while negotiating which of His commands we will follow?
Perhaps because surrender frightens us.
Perhaps because we fear what obedience will cost.
Perhaps because we have confused God's patience with His approval.
Perhaps because we have become so familiar with Christian language that we have forgotten how radical the call to follow Jesus really is.
Or perhaps because there is still something we love more than we are willing to admit.
Whatever the reason, the answer is not found in making a more impressive religious promise.
Peter already tried that.
The answer is found in turning back to Christ.
The Christ who knows our failures.
The Christ who speaks truth without compromise.
The Christ who bore our sins.
The Christ who rose victorious over death.
The Christ who receives repentant sinners.
The Christ who sends His Spirit to transform His people.
The Christ who remains worthy of obedience even when obedience is costly.
One day, we will no longer have to choose between the comfort of this world and the commands of our Savior.
Faith will become sight.
But today, we are still walking.
Still learning.
Still being corrected.
Still depending on grace.
And the question is not whether we can promise Jesus a flawless tomorrow.
It is whether we will trust Him enough to obey what He has already shown us today.
Maybe that means confessing a hidden sin.
Maybe it means seeking reconciliation.
Maybe it means leaving something that has been destroying your spiritual life.
Maybe it means returning to prayer after months of silence.
Maybe it means finally opening the Bible you have been quoting but not allowing to correct you.
Maybe it means falling to your knees and admitting that the greatest obstacle in your discipleship has not been a lack of information.
It has been your unwillingness to surrender.
And if that is where you are, there is still hope.
Jesus did not go to the cross to make sin comfortable.
He went to the cross to save sinners.
He did not rise from the grave merely to become an inspiring figure in our stories.
He rose as the living Lord.
And His invitation still stands.
Two words.
No negotiation.
But an invitation full of grace.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question that no pastor, writer, friend, or stranger can answer for you.
What has Jesus already told me to surrender that I am still trying to negotiate?
Do not rush to answer publicly.
First, answer Him.
Let it be the beginning of an honest prayer, not a claim of perfection.
Because the goal is not merely that people call Jesus Lord.
It is that people come to know Him, trust Him, love Him, and follow Him.
Your scandal may be real.
Your failure may be painful.
Your compromise may have lasted longer than you ever imagined.
But the final chapter does not have to belong to your sin.
It can belong to the grace of Jesus Christ.
The hands you have been resisting are the very hands that were pierced to bring you home.
